Chapter 32:

Azusa and Honoka's "performance" for the day was a merciless torture aimed at their feet. Among the assembled demons were families that the sisters had once exorcised—the Ox Demon clan with their gloomy gazes, the Shadow Fiends restlessly shifting in the darkness, and grotesque mountain spirits and ogres.
Their pale, delicate feet were firmly secured by mechanical devices, hoisted high like treasures on display. Several cold suction cups extended from the apparatus, precisely latching onto their toes and slowly exerting pressure, prying each toe wide apart to expose the most tender, vulnerable skin hidden between them.

Their toenails had been meticulously painted—Azusa's in a soft blue, Honoka's in a vivid red. The colors gleamed starkly in the dim light, like malicious ornaments, accentuating their helplessness and rendering their shame utterly undeniable.

"Don't they look much cuter this way?" some demon snickered from the crowd.

Azusa clenched her jaw tightly; Honoka, however, forced out a defiant smirk, trying to mask the fear surging in her eyes with that feigned bravado. Both knew this was only the beginning.
Then, the bizarre instruments—their tips as soft as brushes, yet emitting a low mechanical hum like a chainsaw at their base—were precisely inserted into the gaps between their splayed toes.
Azusa's toes instinctively curled, but the suction cups held them fast, leaving her no choice but to endure those vibrating bristles pressing into the most sensitive skin between her digits. The simultaneous assault of cold contact and mechanical tremor made her body tense instantly, a stifled groan escaping from deep in her throat.
Honoka's defiant smirk froze the moment the instrument touched the spaces between her toes. The humming sound seemed to bore into her consciousness like a drill, and wherever the brushes swept, ticklish sensations shot up like electric currents. Her toes twitched helplessly, only driving the bristles deeper into those vulnerable regions that had never been touched before.
Below, the demons that the sisters had once exorcised held their breath.
Suddenly, the finger-like brushes began to vibrate and spin, and the chainsaw-like brushes started rotating as well. The fine bristles trembled at high speed between their toes, like countless invisible hands simultaneously scraping their most vulnerable skin.
Both sisters' composure shattered almost simultaneously.
Azusa's clenched jaw was the first to give way—a stifled whimper squeezed from deep in her throat, quickly escalating into uncontrollable, hysterical laughter. Her body convulsed violently within its restraints, her toes futilely curling and splaying, only driving the rotating bristles deeper into the gaps between them.
Honoka's barely maintained defiant smirk completely disintegrated. She threw her head back, laughter tearing through her throat like ripping fabric, mixed with gasps and strangled breaths. Her feet twitched spasmodically in the mechanical apparatus, each vibration sending her laughter further into chaos.
Below, the demons' cheers intertwined with the sisters' crumbling laughter, echoing throughout the entire torture chamber.
Tears sprang to their eyes almost instantly. They had long known—from the very first day of their captivity, from the moment the tickling torture had first shattered their consciousness—that they were utterly incapable of enduring this torment.
But knowing, and being forced to face it again, were two entirely different things.
Azusa's tears mingled with sweat as they rolled down her cheeks, fresh moisture continuously seeping from beneath her tightly shut eyelids. Her laughter had grown hoarse, tinged with sobs, like the death cry of some wounded creature.
Honoka's defiant smirk had vanished without a trace, replaced by an expression of complete collapse. Her head was thrown back, tears tracing paths down the curve of her neck, laughter and weeping merging into something indistinguishable.
Their bodies remembered. Remembered the terror of every ticklish touch, the shudder that ran through every inch of skin when stimulated, remembered how they had lost dignity, reason, everything—all in helpless laughter.
And now, they could only endure it all over again.
After what felt like an eternity, the tickling between their toes finally stopped.
Azusa and Honoka sagged limply in their restraints, chests heaving violently, gasping for air in great, desperate gulps. Their splayed toes hung limply, the skin between them still throbbing with that tingling after-sensation—as if countless tiny electric currents still crackled just beneath the surface.
"Can't even handle a little toe-tickling? Pathetic…"
"Weren't you two all high and mighty as exorcists? Now you can't even stand this much?"
"Look at them, flopping like fish out of water, hahaha—"
The demons' taunts came from all directions, dripping with mockery, contempt, and malice. Every word pierced clearly into their ears, but they had no strength left to respond—not even enough strength left to feel ashamed.
All they could do was use this brief respite to breathe.
Like drowning victims finally breaking the surface, even if only for a few seconds.
The demons didn't let them rest for long.
Before their breathing could fully settle, something cold pressed against their soles—something was being attached.
Azusa's body tensed instantly. She couldn't see what it was, only feel its bizarre texture: a flat surface, but covered in countless… protrusions? Like tiny rounded tips pressing simultaneously into the most sensitive skin of her feet.
"Wh-what is…?" She tried to speak, but only broken, breathless sounds emerged.
Honoka felt it too. The thing was applied lightly, almost weightless, yet the fact that she couldn't see it multiplied her fear tenfold. Her toes twitched involuntarily, trying to escape the unknown sensation, only pressing those countless tiny bumps more distinctly into her soles.
All they could do was wait.
Wait for the demons to reveal—this time, what awaited them.
"Aahaha! It tickles—!"
Almost simultaneously, the maddening tickling sensation returned to the spaces between their toes, while the countless tiny bumps on their soles began vibrating intensely. The dual assault of ticklishness flooded their reason like a tidal wave.
Azusa's head snapped back, uncontrollable laughter tearing from her throat like screams. Her toes twitched futilely within the suction cups' grip, the bristles between them and the vibrating bumps on her soles tormenting her most vulnerable areas simultaneously.
Honoka's last remaining shred of composure crumbled in an instant. She laughed until her whole body trembled, tears spraying with each convulsion, saliva mixing with sweat and tears at the corners of her mouth. Her feet spasmed helplessly within the apparatus, unable to escape a single sensation.
This tickling—this torture that burrowed from the depths between their toes into their very marrow, while simultaneously crawling up from their soles through every nerve—plunged them back into the abyss of helpless hysterics in an instant.
Sweat slid down their violently trembling bodies—from tensed calves, along inner thighs; or over their collarbones and heaving chests, finally pooling in spasming stomachs. Each droplet glistened in the dim light, as if their crumbling dignity had condensed into visible form.
Their feet were especially drenched, the spaces between their forcibly splayed toes slick with moisture, creating a sticky contrast against the cold machinery that made every vibration more intense, more unbearable.
The girls' laughter echoed through the chamber—hoarse, broken, yet piercing the air like shards of glass.
Below, the demons' excitement reached its peak. They clapped, stomped, unleashed all manner of strange cheers. Those demon families that had once been exorcised by the sisters now watched with vengeful ecstasy gleaming in their eyes. The Ox Demons' heavy breathing mingled with laughter, Shadow Fiends twisted and danced in the darkness, Mountain Spirits bared their fangs in bone-chilling grins.
For them, nothing could be more satisfying than witnessing their former enemies collapse so completely.
Amidst the chaos of hysterical laughter, no one noticed—the mechanical arms extended silently, their tips aiming at the sisters' completely unprotected heels. Now those two spots trembled with each spasm of their bound feet, sweat tracing slow paths along the curve of their heels, glistening helplessly in the dim light.
The mechanical hands paused for a second, as if savoring their prey's complete unawareness.
Then, they slowly descended.
And Azusa and Honoka continued laughing, tears blurring their vision, their ears filled only with the noise of their own crumbling laughter intertwined with the demons' cheers from below. They didn't know—a new threat was already inches away.
The moment the mechanical hands made contact with their heels, their fractured laughter shattered into something else entirely—
"AHHH——!!"
It was a sound somewhere between a scream and a wail, torn violently from the gaps between their hysterical laughter. The stimulation on their heels was far more intense, far more unbearable than anything on their soles. Every vibration from the machinery felt like it was directly stimulating their nerve endings.
Azusa's body arched like a shrimp, only to be crushed back down by her restraints, leaving her to convulse futilely within her limited range. Her laughter had completely distorted, pitched so high it barely sounded human, mixed with strangulated gasps.
Honoka thrashed her head wildly from side to side, tears and sweat spraying through the air. She wanted to scream, to curse, to beg—but every sound that escaped could only emerge as more hysterical laughter. Her feet spasmed helplessly against the machinery's manipulations, unable to avoid a single touch.
And below—
"Hahaha! Yes! Just like that!"
"Look at them! The great exorcists? Ha!"
"Scream! Scream louder!"
The demons' cheers and laughter rose and fell in waves, their sinister, sadistic gleams flicker in the dim light like beasts surrounding dying prey. Every broken note, every convulsion, every tear from the sisters became the most exquisite seasoning for this bloody狂欢.
No mercy. No sympathy.
Only pure, boiling sadistic delight.
" Pleasure.
Before they could catch their breath from the heel torment, the rolling brushes for the balls of their feet were applied as well.
Row upon row of fine, dense bristles precisely covered every inch of skin from the base of their toes to the front of their arches. As they began to roll, that tickling—that sensation burrowing through every pore simultaneously, exploding along every nerve—utterly shredded whatever remnants of sanity they had left.
Azusa's body jerked violently as if electrocuted, her waist twisting futilely, her legs spasming within their restraints. Her laughter had completely gotten out of control, high-pitched and shattered, mixed with near-suffocating gasps and sobs.
Animalistic wails tearing from deep in Honoka's throat—only to be immediately swallowed by hysterical laughter. Her feet curled and splayed unconsciously beneath the rolling brushes' torment, only driving those fine soft bristles deeper into every crease.
They writhed. They struggled. They cried. They laughed.
But they couldn't escape an inch.
"So these are the great exorcists of the Kuromyamai house? Hahaha!!"
The demons' mockery rose from below like a vicious slap, yet it didn't even leave room for shame—because they had long lost all capacity for conscious perception amidst their laughter, leaving only their bodies' most primal, most humiliating responses.

Tentacles climbed onto their insteps, sparing no hidden ticklish spot—the hollows where toes meet the foot, even the paper-thin vulnerable skin on the inside of their ankles. Every inch of skin was explored as if licked gently, each undulation bringing new, unpredictable waves of ticklish sensation.
Azusa's toes splayed and curled helplessly within their suction cups, the skin of her insteps rippling with fine tremors at the tentacles' touch. Her laughter had grown hoarse to the point of suffocation; through tear-blurred vision, she could only watch those dark tendrils crawled slowly over her feet, like some nightmare from which there was no waking.
Honoka's feet convulsed violently, trying to kickand flail but only ended up shaking in vain. The tentacles tightened further, as if mocking her struggles. Their soft tips burrowed between her toes, into every minute crease of her insteps, into every sensitive spot she could imagine—and places she couldn't.
Not a single ticklish spot was spared.
Not a single chance of escape remained.
The suction cups were replaced with specialized rotating brushes.
Those devices that had firmly held their toes were now substituted with fine, spinning brush heads—each toe individually encased, the bristles attacked the tip, the pad, the base, even the sensitive edges where nail met skin that were likely overlooked.
As the brush heads began to spin, that concentrated, meticulous ticklish sensation exploded from ten points simultaneously.
Azusa's toes trembled helplessly within the brush wrapping, each toe enduring its own private torment. She wanted to curl, to avoid, but the brush heads clung tight, the spinning bristles sparing not a millimeter of skin. Her laughter had shattered into something beyond words, leaving only staccato gasps and convulsive inhalations.
Honoka's toes jerked violently, like ten nerve bundles being electrocuted at once. Those toes, once painted with red polish, now trembled in the dim light with each rotation of the brushes, every spin making her body tense tighter and her laughter climb higher.
Each cute little toe was being individually "serviced."
Each wave of ticklishness could not be shared, could not be shared to the others.
And this "performance" still had a very long time to go.
Chapter 33:

Yoko Yaminein had prepared for this rescue for a long time.

It wasn’t that she lacked confidence in her own abilities. But her aunt and mentor—Nana Yaminein—had fallen. Her mother, Akemi Yaminein, had fallen too. Both had vanished without a trace. She had never witnessed her mother’s skill firsthand, but from the rare glimpses in her aunt’s tone, she understood that the woman had once been a formidable exorcist. And Nana Yaminein was the strongest exorcist she knew.

If they could disappear into this place without a sound, Yoko dared not underestimate it. She couldn’t simply walk through the front gate.

Months of investigation had mapped every patrol route, every shift change, even the thickness of the walls. Her mother, her teacher, her two younger cousins—Honoka and Azusa—were inside. She had confirmed it, over and over, until there was no room for doubt.

Tonight, under the faintest sliver of moonlight, she made her final preparations and slipped in.

She kept low, her fingers sinking into the cold, damp soil. The stench of rot and rust clung to the back of her throat, an unshakeable film. She let out a slow breath and tightened her grip on the short knife at her waist. The cloth wrapped around the hilt was soaked through with sweat.

She thought of her aunt’s face. Those steady, unwavering eyes had once told her, in the middle of training: “Your mother is stronger than you think.”

That was all.

Now even those eyes were gone, swallowed by this place.

Yoko wet her cracked lips and peered past the broken wall ahead. In the darkness, the demon stronghold lay like a crouching beast, exhaling its foul breath in slow, steady pulses. Footsteps sounded in the distance—heavy, dragging something metallic across the stone. She counted the beats, waited for the sound to turn down a corridor, and then darted from her hiding spot.

Her feet touched the ground with barely a whisper. She hugged the wall, her back pressed flat against the cold, slick stone, the knife reversed against her forearm. Her breathing was so shallow she could hardly hear it herself.

There was no turning back.
She dragged the monster’s corpse as far as she could into the shadows by the wall, her movements so controlled even the rustle of her clothes was barely audible.
Greenish blood traced the blade’s edge before she flicked her wrist, sending a few droplets spattering to the ground where they disappeared into the dust.
She did not move immediately. Holding her breath, she listened.
Only the low moan of wind slipping through cracks in the walls, and the faint beat of her own heart.
Her soles pressed flat to the floor, stepping without so much as a crunch of gravel.
She flowed along the wall like a shred of darkness, soundless.
One corner, then another. At each turn, she paused for a heartbeat, her gaze slipping around the edge before her body followed, scanning the corridor beyond for any sign of disturbance.
Her fingertips tingled.
Not fear—just the tautness of holding her breath too long.
Ahead was the spot she had spent weeks verifying: an iron door set into the stone wall, the rust on its handle exactly as she investigation.
She crouched beside it, pressing her spine flat against the cold rock. With her right hand, she pressed it to her chest and slowed her breathing one last time.
When she finally reached the cell where her two elders were imprisoned—the so-called “Chamber of Atonement”—the sight before her made her breath catch for a moment.
She crouched outside the iron bars and peered cautiously into the dimly lit space.
Inside, the two women were encased in blocks of a cement-like substance that gave off a faint purplish-red. Its surface was rough, clearly some kind of demonic construct. They were almost entirely sealed within, unable to move. Only their heads, feet, breasts, and buttocks remained exposed.
It was her mother and her aunt.
Their heads drooped limply, eye masks covering their faces. Sweat and traces of some dried, milky fluid clung to their skin. There were no external wounds on their exposed flesh, but the signs of prolonged abuse were unmistakable—reddish marks like fingerprints pressed into their breasts, streaks of viscous, still-damp fluid trailing down the insides of their thighs.
Their chests rose and fell faintly. They were alive. Barely.
Yoko clenched her jaw, her fists tightening against her knees.
She made no sound. She simply stared at those familiar faces, swallowing down whatever was rising in her throat, one breath at a time.
Yoko’s gaze traveled lower, and then she saw it all—around their necks, dark silver rings pressed tight against the skin, their surfaces etched with dense rows of咒文. Even the faint rise and fall of their throats seemed held in check by them.
But it didn’t end there.
Metal rings pierced through their nipples, catching the weak light with a cold gleam. Smaller ones were set into their clitorises, the skin around them red and raw. Each ring trailed faint traces of spiritual residue, writhing slowly like something alive.
Her fingertips went numb.
It wasn’t fear. It was something colder, sinking from her chest down to the pit of her stomach, weighing so heavily that her knees nearly buckled.
Her mother and her aunt didn’t even have the strength to hide themselves. Or to tremble. They were simply there, sealed inside those purplish-red blocks, discarded like objects worn out from use.
She bit down hard on her lip until the taste of iron spread across her tongue.
Fortunately, there were no demons in the cell at that moment, no one there to torment them. A so-called “rest period,” perhaps.
Yoko approached the purplish-red block and reached out to touch its surface—cold, hard. The moment her fingertips made contact, a faint pulse of spiritual power pushed back, like the prick of a fine needle. She clenched her jaw and tried to wedge her short blade into the edge. It bit in for barely a finger’s width before jamming solid. She pushed at the base of the block, but it didn’t budge, as if it had grown from the floor itself.
She stopped. Her fists pressed against her knees. Sweat beaded on her forehead.
She couldn’t break it open. Couldn’t move it.
She knew this was a window of opportunity—the demons were absent, the silence a stolen gift. But she was helpless against this thing.
She forced herself to calm down, to study the block’s structure again, when a faint sound came from behind her—the involuntary twitch of a body held too long in place.
She jerked her head up.
Her mother’s head had turned slightly. That face, half-covered by an eyepatch, angled toward her. Even through the patch, Yoko could feel the gaze cutting into her—and then her mother’s head began to move, left and right. Small motions, but frantic, as if using the last dregs of strength she had left.
Go. Leave.
It was then that Yoko noticed their mouths. Both were fixed open with gags—metal frames clamped between their teeth, lips stretched into a rigid shape, not a single sound able to escape. It wasn’t that they didn’t want to speak. They couldn’t.
Aunt Nana stirred slightly beside her. Her eyelids fluttered, as though trying to open them, but she couldn’t muster even that much.
Yoko stared at her mother, still shaking her head. Something clenched tight around her chest, squeezing. She opened her mouth, but no sound came. She held that exhausted face in her gaze, her nails digging into her palms.
She understood what her mother was trying to tell her.
Chapter 34:
Yoko crouched in the shadows of the cell, her nails nearly digging into her palms.
She watched her mother shaking her head—so desperate, so hopeless, like a dull blade slicing back and forth across her chest. Her aunt could barely muster the strength to shake her head anymore. Her eyelids fluttered a few times, but never opened.
She couldn’t stay here. She knew that.
But she didn’t want to leave either.
Her fists clenched and unclenched. In the end, it was the faint glimmer of wetness welling up from her mother’s half-closed eye that finally pushed her to her feet.
You can’t save us. Go.
The corridor was darker than when she had come in.
She kept low, moving swiftly along the wall, her soles gliding over the floor, each step landing precisely where her previous one had fallen. Her breathing was short, held to the shallowest rhythm. Her eyes searched every corner, every crack in the darkness.
But the air had changed.
Too quiet. Even the low moan of wind through the crevices was gone.
She stopped, pressing her back flat against the stone wall, and slowly drew her short blade.
They’re coming.
Not from one direction. From two. From three. Faint, hard sounds—like chitin scraping against stone—seeped out of the depths of the corridor, from the path she had come from, from the path ahead, from the corners she thought she had already cleared.
She had been discovered.
Yoko narrowed her eyes, shifted her grip on the blade, and exhaled a stale breath.
Come on, then. At least not in that cell. At least not in front of them.
She had lost count of how many times she had swung the two kodachi.
Fighting her way out of the cell block, Yoko’s breathing had grown shallow and rapid. She had no time to flick the green blood off the blades—layer upon layer of it had dripped past the guards and onto her fingers, sticky and slick, making it almost impossible to keep a firm grip on the hilts. She didn’t stop to wipe them clean. There was no time.
Sounds came from both behind and ahead. The scrape of hard chitin against stone walls. The wet drag of flesh across the floor. And those shrill cries—like infants, like beasts—pouring from the depths of the corridor, growing in number, drawing closer.
She burst around a corner and drove her left-hand kodachi into the throat of a demon lunging from the side. The creature didn’t even have time to scream. Its body went limp, slumping against her. She shoved it off with her knee, and the blade came free with a dull, wet sound, spraying green fluid across half her face. At the same time, she swung her right-hand blade upward, severing the forelimb of another demon dropping from above.
No time to catch her breath.
She ducked under a third demon’s charge, stumbled, and slammed her knee into the ground. Before she could rise, she swung one blade upward in a reverse grip, piercing through the soft underside of its jaw. The other blade swept to her side, just in time to parry a claw reaching from behind—metal and chitin scraped together with a shrill shriek.
Yoko pushed herself up, gasping. Her left shoulder burned—she couldn’t remember when it had happened. Her clothes were torn, skin laid open, blood trailing down her arm. Both kodachi were drenched in green blood, the gleam of their steel swallowed by the viscous fluid, leaving only heavy, cold iron.
The exit was close.
She could feel it. Not the thin draft squeezing through cracks in the wall, but real wind—wind from outside, carrying the chill of earth and night. It poured through some invisible gap ahead, brushing against her blood-soaked face like a cold slap.
She clenched her teeth and kept running toward it. Her steps grew heavier, but she didn’t slow. Both blades hung loose at her sides, their tips dragging across the ground, leaving two thin, long trails of blood behind her.
The sounds of pursuit were still behind her. But fewer than before. Not because they had given up—but because any that could keep up had already fallen somewhere along the path she had carved.
The two kodachi moved in her hands with unnerving steadiness.
The demon lunging from the front didn’t even have time to open its mouth before the blade had already passed through its throat. Yoko’s feet didn’t stop. Her breathing didn’t even waver. A shift of her body, a sliding step, and her left-hand blade swept sideways—another demon’s forelimb, along with half its shoulder, spun into the air. Green blood traced an arc. She didn’t bother to look.
These small fry were no match for her.
Fighting her way from the cell block to here, she had picked up a few scratches. But none were fatal—none had even been unavoidable. She simply hadn’t needed to avoid them. She was faster than them. Sharper. More ruthless. Every cut was clean, economical, exactly what a trained exorcist should be.
But her heart wasn’t in the blades.
Her mother’s face. Her mouth stretched open by the gag. That half-closed eye beneath the eyepatch, shaking its head—go. Her aunt couldn’t even muster the strength to shake her head anymore. Her eyelids fluttered faintly, but never opened. The rings through their nipples, through their clitorises—glinting coldly in the dim cell, like needles driven into flesh. Driven into the back of her eyes as well.
Yoko clenched her jaw and forced a stale breath out through her nose.
Her left-hand blade flashed upward, splitting open the belly of a demon dropping from above. Her right foot slid half a step back, and her right-hand blade punched through the skull of another creature lunging from the side. The movements were clean. Not a single unnecessary tremor.
Her face was calm. Almost blank.
Only her fingers—wrapped around the hilts—had gone white, knuckles stretched tight as if about to crack.
She couldn’t afford to lose control. Couldn’t afford to rush. Couldn’t fall here.
The exit was close. Wind was already pouring in—cool against her cheek. Like her mother’s hand. No—not like that. Her mother’s hand had never been this cold. Never this cruel.
Yoko crossed both blades in front of her chest, then flicked them outward at the same time. Green blood sprayed from the edges, splattering against the stone walls and leaving two thin streaks. She took a deep breath and stepped toward the exit.

Two hours had passed.
The stone floor before the exit was soaked with blood.
The Blue Ogre King lay face-down. The hole in its chest was hidden beneath its body, invisible from above. It lay motionless, limbs sprawled, like a collapsed mountain of flesh. Its spiked club had rolled a few paces away, several of the iron spikes broken off, thick with dark green blood.
The Lizardman slumped against the wall, half-sitting, half-lying. A long gash ran from its left shoulder to its right ribs—scales peeled back, exposing the dark red meat beneath. It was still alive. Its vertical pupils were half open, the tip of its tail twitching occasionally, but it couldn’t move anymore.
Yoko sat in the middle of the blood.
A thin line of blood hung from the corner of her mouth, half-dried, trailing from her lower lip to her chin. She didn’t bother to wipe it away.
Both kodachi were chipped and dulled. The left one was stuck into a crack in the stone beside her, the blade twisted, the edge curled back like a jagged saw. Green blood dripped slowly down the spine. The right one was still in her hand. The cloth wrapped around the hilt was completely soaked through, its original color impossible to tell. The blade had lost several chunks along its edge— looked like a row of uneven teeth.
The strap of one of the geta sandals snapped and fell to the ground.
She tried to stand.
Her knee lifted halfway before the muscles in her thigh seized violently, and she collapsed back down. Her spine hit a shard of broken stone, forcing a pained grunt from her throat. She didn’t try again.
The walls were splattered with blood. Hers, and the demons’.
Dark red spray marks stretched from the base of the wall up to about chest height. Some were five-fingered claw marks. Others were fan-shaped spatters from blunt impacts. Long smear trails ran diagonally from the wall down to the floor—as if something had been dragged down, fingers desperately scraping for purchase. Greens, reds, deep browns—all mixed together, indistinguishable in the faint moonlight.
The silence was like a grave, broken only by the wind pouring in from outside, brushing over the blood-soaked ground and the scattered scales with a soft, whispering rustle.
When she opened her eyes again, the first thing she saw was the rough stone ceiling.
Consciousness came back to her slowly, heavily, like being pulled up from the bottom of a muddy swamp. She instinctively tried to push herself up—her hands were tied behind her back. The coarse rope bit deep into the flesh of her wrists. She gave a small tug—the knot didn’t budge, and the friction burned her skin like fire.
She tried to draw on her spiritual energy.
Nothing.
Her core was empty. Hollowed out, as if someone had scraped it clean—not a single shred of power remained.
No. Not empty. Sealed.
She lowered her gaze and saw it around her neck. A dull silver metal ring, clamped tight on her neck. Its surface was covered in dense spells—the same kind she had seen on her aunt and her mother. A sealing collar. The cold metal pressed against her skin, digging in slightly with each swallow, like something alive slowly tightening its grip.
Her breath stopped for a moment.
Not from fear. From something heavier, colder—sinking from her chest all the way down to the pit of her stomach.
She closed her eyes. Opened them again.
The ceiling was still there. The ropes were still there. The collar was still there.
She lay still, no longer struggling. Just shifted her gaze from the ceiling, slowly scanning her surroundings—walls, floor, iron bars. The air was thick with the smell of damp mold, mixed with faint traces of rust and decay.
The same kind of cell as her mother’s.
A blue ogre and a lizardman stepped into the cell.
No words were exchanged. No glances, no pause, no warning.
The two monsters' rough, massive hands grabbed the fabric at her chest—the outer garment, the tight-fitting ninja suit beneath it, and the layer underneath all at once. Two layers of cloth tore apart. The sound of ripping fabric was unnaturally loud in the cramped cell. Shreds of cloth hung from her shoulders and waist, dangling like rags.
Her heavy, full breasts, freed from their bindings, sprang loose. They swayed slightly in the dim light.
The lizardman stood to the side. Its vertical pupils reflected her exposed upper body, its gaze sliding slowly from her collarbone down to her chest—expressionless, motionless, just watching.
Yoko closed her eyes. A fine layer of goosebumps rose on her skin.
Her eyelashes fluttered once, and her lips pressed into a thin line. At the corner of her mouth, a dried streak of blood from the earlier fight still remained. Her breathing was shallow but steady. Her chest rose and fell with that rhythm, the soft pale flesh shifting in the faint light, drawing subtle shadows of motion.
The ogre let out a low, rumbling growl—as if confirming something, or simply pushing air from its throat. It didn’t touch her again. It crouched down, bringing its face closer, its murky yellow eyes fixed on her bare breasts. Its breath hit her skin—carrying the stench of rotting meat and blood.

When Yoko woke up, the first thing she felt wasn’t pain. It was cold.
The air clung to her bare skin, damp and chill as a thin layer of ice. She instinctively tried to curl up—but her body didn’t move. Not from weakness. From restraint.
She opened her eyes and lifted her head slightly.
Her hands were tied behind her back, her wrists sunk deep into the purplish-red mass, completely immobile. Her legs were in a kneeling position—her knees pressed against the rough stone floor, but from the middle of the block, her lower legs extended outward, her feet left hanging in the air. Her toes touched nothing but the cold emptiness around them.
Her upper body was bent backward. A spiked club protruded diagonally from the purplish-red block behind her, its haft embedded solidly in the stone-like substance. Its tip pressed exactly against her back—above her waist, below her shoulder blades. The club was rough and heavy, caked with dried dark green gore, like a rigid arm stubbornly shoving her spine forward. Her entire body was stretched into the shape of a drawn bow by that fixed implement—her lower back forced outward, her chest thrust high and forward, heavy and prominent, trembling faintly with each shallow breath.
She wore not a single piece of clothing. Her skin was directly exposed to the damp, cold air of the cell, every part of her clearly visible.
